notes: The analysis shows the thesis defeated by two active objections and resting on four unsupported, high-risk assumptions. The undercutting objection (oligopoly collapse) attacks the claim that the hybrid neutralises coercion and exclusion; the enhanced thesis concedes this by making the resolution conditional and splitting the objections the hybrid does neutralise (compromise, Sybil, unfamiliar credentials) from those it only relocates absent anti-consolidation measures. The rebutting objection (scope misunderstanding) attacks the existence of the core itself; rather than ignoring it, the enhanced thesis names it as the live escape route and relocates the residual disagreement to a sharper question — whether cross-application uniqueness is a genuine requirement for the relevant use cases — which also surfaces the previously silent assumption 'one-person-one-identity is required'. The unsupported characterisation and shared-rejection assumptions are made explicit as a 'provided that' condition; the feasibility-at-scale assumption for a shared uniqueness check is stated inline. The core direction (partly a misunderstanding, uniqueness/revocation as the substantive residue, hybrid resolves the periphery not the center) is preserved, but the claim is now defensible against the two defeaters rather than defeated by them.
